## Collaborative Notes

The Fall 2026 collaborative notes supplement the instructor-authored
*Introduction to Data Science* book. They give students practice explaining
data-science concepts and working through a Git and GitHub review process.

The notes are maintained in the
[`ids-f26` repository](https://github.com/statds/ids-f26). Students contribute
through topic branches and pull requests. Each topic contribution consists of:

1. a RevealJS slide deck in its own directory under `presentations/`; and
2. a short catalog entry in the relevant topical chapter.

The slide deck is the substantive contribution. Students are not expected to
rewrite their slides as a prose chapter. The topical chapters organize and
link to presentations; they do not duplicate the instructor book.

## Presentation Expectations

A presentation should ordinarily contain:

- a motivating question or explanation of why the topic matters;
- the main concept, method, or tool;
- at least one minimal, reproducible example;
- an interpretation of important output;
- limitations, common mistakes, or situations where the method is unsuitable;
- two or three principal takeaways; and
- sources and image attribution.

Slides should support an oral presentation without becoming a transcript.
Use readable text, explain displayed code and output, and generate results
from executable code when practical. Link to relevant material in `ids-book`
instead of repeating substantial instructor-authored exposition.

The
[example Quarto presentation](presentations/example-quarto-presentations/)
demonstrates the expected directory layout and basic slide conventions.

## Topic Presentations

The private course syllabus contains the assessment policies for topic
presentations. This public chapter documents the presentation order, topic
options, schedule, and contribution workflow without reproducing grading
details.

### Presentation Order

The topic presentation order will be finalized in class. Each student will
contribute one digit to the random seed. The current seed produces a
provisional order; after the contributed digits replace it, the same seed will
reproduce the final order on every render.

```{python}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
import csv

with open("roster.txt", newline="") as file:
    roster = csv.DictReader(file, delimiter="\t")
    presenters = [
        f"{row['Last Name']}, {row['First Name']}"
        for row in roster
    ]

import random

## seed jointly set by the class, with one digit from each student
random.seed(0)  # replace 0 with the sum of the contributed digits
random.sample(presenters, len(presenters))
```

The displayed order is provisional until the class sets the seed. The final
order will establish priority for topic selection and the default sequence for
topic presentations. Some topics have prerequisites, so the instructor may
adjust the schedule. Students may exchange slots by mutual agreement. Record
an approved change through a pull request and notify the instructor.

## Contributing to the Collaborative Notes

Use the following workflow:

1. Synchronize your local repository with the shared repository.
2. Create and switch to a topic branch.
3. Copy and adapt the example presentation directory.
4. Add a short entry to the appropriate topical chapter.
5. Activate the course Python environment when computation is required.
6. Render and review the presentation locally.
7. Make small commits with informative messages.
8. Push the branch and open a pull request.
9. Respond to review and revise the contribution as needed.

Before requesting review, check that the contribution:

- is original and properly attributes all sources;
- follows the example presentation structure and has a matching chapter entry;
- follows the repository's file-naming and source-writing conventions;
- keeps lines reasonably short;
- uses BibTeX for scholarly references;
- avoids unnecessary external files and large data files;
- uses only images that may legally be redistributed;
- records any new Python dependencies in the environment specification; and
- renders successfully on the contributor's computer.

Pull requests contain source files, not rendered output. After a pull request
is reviewed and merged, the instructor renders the complete notes and all
accepted presentations and publishes the unified site.

Editorial acceptance and course assessment are separate decisions. Assessment
emphasizes the contribution process, including meaningful work, appropriate Git
usage, responsiveness to review, reproducibility, and constructive feedback to
classmates.

## Assignment Workflow

Graded work is submitted through the designated Classroom 50 repository, not
through the instructor book or collaborative-notes repository.

Each assignment submission must use one `.qmd` source file that solves all
assigned problems. Label every problem clearly inside that file so that the
source and rendered PDF are easy to navigate. Use the
[homework template](https://github.com/statds/hw-template) as the starting
point for the required structure.

For each assignment:

1. Accept the assignment using the link provided through the course site.
2. Clone the resulting repository to your computer.
3. Develop the single Quarto source file locally, solve every assigned
   problem, and organize the work into meaningful commits.
4. Push all source files and their complete commit history to your assignment
   repository. A final snapshot without the development history is not a
   complete submission.
5. Render the assignment and submit the PDF for ease of grading, following the
   assignment instructions for where to attach it.

Keep generated files out of the repository unless the assignment explicitly
requests them. Use Git from the command line rather than GitHub's file-upload
interface, and never commit credentials or large data files.

## Syllabus Check

Use the syllabus and its linked resources to answer the following questions.
The questions are intended to clarify course expectations rather than reward
memorization; consult the relevant source when uncertain.

1. Where should you look for private course materials, permanent instructor
   notes, and Fall 2026 student presentations?
2. What percentage of the grade comes from style, participation, homework,
   topic presentations, the midterm project, and the final project? How does
   the final-project requirement differ between STAT 3255 and STAT 5255?
3. How are the 20 topic-presentation points divided among approval and preview,
   the oral presentation, and the pull request? When is each component due?
4. What must a topic-presentation pull request contain?
5. When are the final two instructional weeks, and what attendance and
   participation are required during them?
6. What are the proposal, instructor-meeting, presentation, and final-report
   deadlines for the final project?
7. How does the maximum available homework credit change during the 48 hours
   after a deadline? What happens after 48 hours?
8. What kinds of AI use are encouraged? Which graded components must be
   completed independently, and when must AI use be disclosed?
9. According to the linked
   [email-etiquette guide](https://marktomforde.com/academic/undergraduates/Email-Etiquette.html),
   what greeting, subject line, closing, and identifying information should a
   professional email contain?
10. What should you check before emailing a question whose answer may already
    appear in the syllabus, assignment instructions, or course notes?
11. How long should you ordinarily allow for an email response, and which
    conversations are better handled during office hours?
12. According to [PEP 8](https://peps.python.org/pep-0008/), how many spaces
    should each indentation level use, what line lengths are recommended, and
    where should imports appear?
13. What skills can you practice with
    [Git Exercises](https://gitexercises.fracz.com/), and why are small,
    meaningful commits preferable to one large final commit?
14. What is the difference between collaboration and copying when completing
    homework or a project?
15. Using the UConn Library guides on
    [avoiding plagiarism](https://guides.lib.uconn.edu/plagiarism) and
    [citing sources](https://guides.lib.uconn.edu/citing), what material must
    be quoted, paraphrased, cited, or otherwise attributed?
16. Under UConn's
    [academic-integrity policy](https://policy.uconn.edu/2023/07/11/academic-scholarly-and-professional-integrity-and-misconduct-aspim-policy-on/),
    why are students expected to ask before using an outside resource when an
    assignment does not explicitly authorize it?
17. Read UConn's [Student Code](https://community.uconn.edu/the-student-code/)
    and its
    [academic-integrity appendix](https://community.uconn.edu/the-student-code/the-student-code-appendix-a/).
    What responsibilities do students have for their own work, proper
    attribution, and avoiding an unfair advantage?
18. Why are command-line operation, Git, reproducible code, and Quarto treated
    as data-science skills rather than merely software preferences?
19. What information and demonstrated qualities would help the instructor
    write a useful recommendation letter?
